Meteg after the primary stress

(click a Hebrew word or phrase to toggle its spacing)

A meteg almost always appears before the stressed syllable of its chanted word, but it can also come after the stress. Both ITM and CoS discuss MAS (meteg after the stress). Neither book says how often MAS happens; we find that MAM has 231 of them, over 263,191 chanted words.

First, some definitions: a chanted word can be either a simple word (a word of just one atom) or it can be a compound word (a word of two or more atoms connected by maqaf marks). An atom is a sequence of letters uninterrupted by space, maqaf, or any other punctuation.

Which syllable a chanted word is stressed on is not always obvious, so for our survey of MAS, we use Phonetic MAM, an edition of MAM that marks the stressed syllable of every chanted word.

MAS census by cantillation system

The “prose verses” row in the table below is for the 21 books plus Job's prose frame; the “poetic verses” row is Job's main, poetic section plus all Psalms and the entire book of Proverbs. See the appendix on dually-cantillated passages for how this census handles them.

cant-sys c-words MBS MAS
prose 233,586 13,118 177
poetic 29,605 1,814 54
all 263,191 14,932 231

So a meteg comes before the stress 14,932 times and after it 231 times.

Only about 1.5% of the 15,163 meteg marks counted here come after the stress.

MAS by structural type

Three types of MAS are described in both ITM and CoS. Each type has a condition on the syllable where the meteg falls; type 1 also has a condition on the following chanted word:

  1. an open syllable before a chanted word whose first full syllable is stressed;
  2. a final syllable closed by a guttural
  3. a final closed syllable whose vowel is tsere

This page follows Yeivin's narrower condition for type 3: a final closed syllable with tsere. Breuer's corresponding type (a) covers a long vowel in a closed syllable, so a record that meets Breuer's condition but not Yeivin's remains in misc.

Types 2 and 3 could in principle overlap. In this survey, however, every one of the 56 type-2 records has pataḥ rather than tsere, so none also meets the type-3 condition.

The counts below are mechanical, and a chanted word that doesn't fit one of the three types is left in the “misc” row rather than pushed into the nearest type.

Type Prose Poetic Example
1 112 13 הִנֶּ֣נִּֽי בְנִ֑י
2 33 23 תַּצְמִ֣יחַֽ לָ֑ךְ
3 26 16 וַיָּ֣צֵֽץ
misc (not one of the three types above) 6 2 וַיֹּ֥אמֶֽר ׀ לֹ֖א

Sources for types 1–3

Type ITM CoS
1 §332 §3(j), §§46-47
2 §354 §3(b), §§9-10
3 §338, fed by §308 §3(a), §§5-8

Within misc, misc-almost-type-1 has 1 record. Its initial member is Jer. 46:14: the MAS syllable is open, but the following chanted word's first full syllable is unstressed. An opening simple vocal sheva or xataf vowel is pre-syllabic for the type-1 condition.

Within misc, 3-almost-2 has 1 record. Its initial member is Job 15:35: its chanted word וְיָ֣לֹֽד has a final closed syllable with ḥolam, a long vowel. It fits Breuer's broader type (a), but not Yeivin's tsere type 3.

Within misc, misc-vayomer has 4 records. Each has one PASEQ between the meteg-bearing chanted word and the following chanted word; the individual-cases page shows that context.

For the open-syllable type, ITM §332 describes a chanted word stressed on its penultimate syllable, ending in an open syllable, before a chanted word whose first full syllable is stressed. Yeivin calls it rarely marked, commonest in early manuscripts and absent from printed texts, and CoS Ch. 8 grades it optional — which for Breuer means that no tradition settles it and each naqdan decided for himself.

The guttural type is described in ITM §354 and CoS Ch. 8 type (b), where the last syllable of the chanted word ends in ḥet, ayin or he. A furtive pataḥ counts as a separate syllable here, as it is in Phonetic MAM, so a meteg on that guttural comes out after the stress rather than in it. Breuer calls the type obligatory; Yeivin's statement is narrower, that the mark is sometimes used when the chanted word after it begins with lamed or nun.

Type 3 follows Yeivin's tsere type, described in ITM §338, fed by §308's account of retracted stress: where the stress retracts and a final closed syllable keeps its tsere, that syllable takes the mark, and Yeivin says it is marked in manuscripts and printed texts alike. CoS Ch. 8's corresponding type (a) is wider: it has a long vowel in a closed syllable. The one current record in Breuer's type (a) but not Yeivin's type is the 3-almost-2 record above.

The 231 individual cases are listed separately and can be filtered by type.

The 56 type 2 cases have a separate table whose filter uses the following chanted word's initial consonant.

A new MAS in MAM at Isaiah 23:12

The Holman M23 record says that the Aleppo Codex has a meteg under the mem of the chanted word ק֣וּמִֽי at Isaiah 23:12, where MAM had none. The suggestion was taken, so MAM has the meteg there now, and the comparison forms on the M23 card are what Holman was sent, frozen at the date of his message.

The mark is of the open-syllable type: ק֣וּמִֽי is stressed on its first syllable, ends in an open syllable, and the chanted word after it is stressed on its first full syllable. That is the type both books call optional, and at 125 occurrences it is also the commonest of the three in MAM.

The same verse already had another MAS: לֹא־יָנ֥וּחַֽ, whose last syllable a guttural closes. So Isaiah 23:12 now has two of them, one of each of the two commonest types.

MAM has one other chanted word of exactly this shape, and the individual-cases page names it: ק֥וּמִֽי at Dan. 7:5, with the same open final syllable and the same kind of chanted word after it.

The counts above do not include the meteg of ק֣וּמִֽי. They are taken from the Phonetic MAM edition, which has not been regenerated since MAM gained it, so Isaiah 23:12 is one of the verses where the two texts have parted.

The post-silluq case at 1 Samuel 17:5

A meteg after a silluq would be hard to identify in Unicode, since the two marks are one codepoint.

MAM has no MAS on a silluq word, but 1 Samuel 17:5 does raise this issue in some BHS-derived editions. MAM has the verse-final chanted word נְחֹֽשֶׁת׃ with one U+05BD, the silluq. UXLC 3.9 and WLC 4.22 are BHS-derived transcriptions, and each has a second U+05BD on the final syllable. Their forms are evidence about UXLC and WLC; whether the Leningrad Codex has a second mark must be read from folio F159A, column 3, line 8, where the chanted word stands.

Two of the three types could not occur on a silluq word: types 1 and 2 each require a following chanted word, which a verse-final chanted word does not have. Only type 3 could occur there.

A diagnostic overlapping the three positions

One diagnostic overlaps the three positions rather than adding a fourth: a meteg can share a letter with an accent that marks no stress, which the prepositives, the postpositives, ole and geresh muqdam all do. There are 146 such meteg marks, and each is counted in the group its syllable puts it in, before or after the stress, rather than beside them.

Appendix: dually-cantillated passages

MAM has two cantillations for the two Decalogues and Genesis 35:22. The analyses presented in this document use only the cant-alef cantillation strand for each such passage. The table below shows that this choice has only a tiny effect on the prose MBS count, and no effect on any other analysis.
